Whatever the situation, I always find it helpful to consider it from the other person's point of view. Last year before interview season (I had 22 screeners, 18 callbacks, and 12 offers by the end), I read the book "The essential guide to hiring and getting hired" and it was very helpful.

As far as specific tips, look up common questions and prepare by knowing what story from your life you would use as a response. Don't try to script or memorize answers. Also, if you have a great story you really want to tell, make sure to fit it in. When you speak passionately about something, the interviewer can get a glimpse of your personality and might actually remember you.

If you have more specific questions, feel free to ask.

As a hiring manager, a big tell for me is when I ask what they know about our company or why they want to work for us. There is plenty on the web to get a decent picture, and for the really ambitious, they can learn a whole lot about working for us. When I get a lame response, that tells me the interviewee is lazy, and likely not a good candidate.

Why?? Because every fucking interviewer in the country asks this question, and a job applicant that doesn't know this or is too lazy to prepare, is not the kind of person I want working for me.

I had a lot of luck reaching out to people to learn more about companies before my interviews. Hiring managers seemed to like it when I knew some people at the firm and could answer these kinds of questions by bringing up conversations with people who already work there.

I have a group of people within the company that I would like to give limited admin rights to whichever PC/laptop they are logged into (not just this group of people have full admin to this group of machines). I mainly want to allow them to install their own apps and apply patches/updates, but not remove the machine from the domain.

I am just learning GPO and would appreciate some pointers.
Group policy question: allowing users to have limited local admin rights (x-post from /v/sysadmin)

Are you wanting:

"User01" to only have rights to "Computer01"
"User02" to only have rights to "Computer02"
etc.

or

"User01" to:

  • Have rights to "Computer01" when logged on to "Computer01"
  • Have rights to "Computer02" when logged on to "Computer02"
  • etc.

"User02" to:

  • Have rights to "Computer01" when logged on to "Computer01"
  • Have rights to "Computer02" when logged on to "Computer02"
  • etc.
The second scenario is preferred, but the users rarely switch workstations. In the event of a laptop or PC failure, I could make a manual switch, if necessary.

Here is a write up on that... http://nerddrivel.com/category/active-directory/ scroll to the second article.

The short of it is:

GPO - User Configuration - Preferences - Control Panel Settings - Local Users and Groups "New Local Group"

Action: Update

Group Name: Administrators (built-in)

Click "Add..." click "..." locate user ins the directory, Action: Add to this group, click OK, repeat if you want to add more users... click Apply.

This process will make all the users in said group local admins on any network computer they log into. There are other ways of doing this , but this is the most basic.
